questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a word's denotation from the attitude its connotation carries
questions.stem: A writer describing a famine first drafts "The people were thin" and then changes it to "The people were gaunt." Both words report the same body shape. What has the revision added?

options.text: An evaluative charge, since gauntness carries hunger that thinness does not
A more exact measurement of how much weight each person had lost
options.misconception: reads a change of connotation as an increase in measurement precision

options.text: A claim that the people were born that way rather than reduced to it
options.misconception: reads the revision as a hereditary claim rather than as a word choice

options.text: A quieter line, since the harder consonant slows the sentence for a reader
options.misconception: credits the effect to sound alone and ignores the evaluative import

questions.explanation: A word's denotation is what it names; its connotation is the attitude a reader takes from it. "Thin" names a body shape and stops there, while "gaunt" names the same shape and imports the idea of insufficiency, which is a judgment the writer has chosen to make about the sentence's subject. The tempting reading treats a stronger word as a more accurate one, but no measurement has changed, only the judgment attached to the measurement; the fourth option is right that sound matters and wrong that it is what this revision is doing, because nothing about the consonants or the rhythm has been altered.
questions.hint: Ask what both words mean, and what only one of them implies.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: identify the judgment a single evaluative word carries in a factual report
questions.stem: A report reads: "Eleven complaints were filed against the Rowan Court between March and June, all concerning the heating. The Committee found the building difficult." What work does the word "difficult" do that the count cannot do?

options.text: It attaches a judgment of character to a building, which a tally cannot
It tells the reader the complaints were unfair to the building's staff
options.misconception: reads a judgment about a structure as a verdict on the people inside it

options.text: It confirms that eleven is the highest number the Committee has recorded
options.misconception: infers a record-breaking figure from a word describing the building's nature

options.text: It explains why the Committee delayed publishing its heating findings
options.misconception: hears a characterization as an explanation of a procedural decision

questions.explanation: The count and the word do different jobs. "Eleven complaints ... concerning the heating" is a tally: it bounds what was received and what it was about. "Difficult" is evaluative, and it moves the report from how many to what kind, which is a claim about the building's character and not something any number can carry. The tempting reading wants the word to smuggle in a motive, but the report nowhere links the judgment to the Committee's timing, and wanting a hidden cause behind a characterization is a habit, not a reading of this sentence.
questions.hint: Ask whether a number can say what kind of thing something is.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: show how a verb choice presents an act as ordinary rather than chosen
questions.stem: An invented story says of a theft: "The boy took the brass key from the hook and put it in his pocket, which is a thing that boys near a coast do." What is the sentence doing with the verb it chose?

options.text: Burying the act in a habit, so the theft is offered as ordinary, not chosen
Correcting the reader for suspecting the boy before the habit is named
options.misconception: believes the sentence exists to repair the reader's judgment of the boy

options.text: Showing that the author disapproves of coastal customs
options.misconception: takes a narrator's local habit for the author's judgment on a region

options.text: Proving the narrator honest, since the habit is reported without comment
options.misconception: reads a flat report of a habit as a sign of the narrator's reliability

questions.explanation: "Took" is a verb of ordinary acquisition, and the relative clause that follows turns a single act into a class of acts. That combination is what does the work: the bare verb keeps the theft unremarkable, and the habit clause then supplies a warrant for the unremarkableness, so a deliberate act arrives dressed as a regional custom. The tempting reading credits the sentence with sincerity, but a flat tone proves nothing about a narrator's accuracy; the fourth option also mistakes a narrator's self-exculpation for the author's opinion, which the sentence never states.
questions.hint: Ask whether the boy is presented as choosing the act.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what a periodic sentence withholds from the reader and until when
questions.stem: A sentence reads: "The cart, its axle groaning, its load of wet coal slumping with every rut, its driver asleep since the long ascent, drew up at the ford just after dawn." What does the shape of that sentence do?

options.text: It postpones the main clause, so the reader reaches the subject only at the end
It lists the cart's parts in the order a mechanic would inspect them
options.misconception: reads a delaying structure as a practical inspection sequence

options.text: It proves the driver slept, since the detail is given without any hedging
options.misconception: treats an unhedged embedded detail as the sentence's main assertion

options.text: It makes the sunrise happen later in the story than it otherwise would
options.misconception: confuses a delay inside a sentence with a change in narrated time

questions.explanation: In a periodic sentence the main clause arrives last, and the reader must hold the subordinate material in suspension until it does. Here three absolute phrases modify "the cart" before the reader is told what the cart did, so the sequence of arriving is built into the sequence of understanding. The tempting reading offers an inspection order, but nothing in the sentence is being inspected; the third and fourth options both confuse the reader's delay inside the sentence with the time of events in the story, which dawn does not slow.
questions.hint: Ask which word in the sentence is the main verb, and where it stands.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: compare a periodic and a loose version of one sentence and locate the difference
questions.stem: Two versions of a report sentence are offered. Version 1: "When the sluice was finally raised, the water went down the channel." Version 2: "The water went down the channel when the sluice was finally raised." What does Version 1 withhold that Version 2 delivers at once?

options.text: Which action is the main one, held back until the opening clause names it
Whether the channel was dry, which the raised sluice confirms in the ending
options.misconception: believes the postponement conceals a fact about the channel's condition

options.text: Why the sluice was raised, which neither version ever supplies
options.misconception: expects a delayed sentence to contain a motive it never promises

options.text: Whether the writer approves of the water's departure from the channel
options.misconception: reads word order as carrying a stance the sentence never voices

questions.explanation: Version 2 puts the subject and its verb first, so the reader knows the main action at once and receives the timing as a supplement. Version 1 begins with a subordinate clause and makes the sluice the reader's first concern, so the water's action is the thing being held back. The tempting readings look for a withheld fact, a withheld motive, or a withheld opinion, but sentence order here withholds nothing about the channel, the sluice's reasons, or the writer's stance; it withholds only which action the sentence is built around.
questions.hint: Ask which version names its subject before its verb.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: choose the revision that preserves a delaying structure while cutting words
questions.stem: A writer has: "The lamp on the pier had been burning since the tide turned, and by the time she reached the last of the steps her shadow was longer than the light." Which revision best keeps what the sentence was doing?

options.text: Keep the since-clause, since it is what makes the second clause land as arrival
Cut the since-clause, since the lengthening shadow already carries the delay
options.misconception: believes one concrete image can carry the whole temporal structure

options.text: Replace the shadow clause with a plain note that she arrived late
options.misconception: trades the image for a summary of the fact the image was doing

options.text: Move the shadow clause to the front, since moving a clause keeps any delay
options.misconception: assumes relocation rather than removal preserves a delaying structure

questions.explanation: The sentence's work is done by two durations laid against each other: the lamp's long burning and the shadow's late lengthening. The since-clause is the measure of the first, and without it the reader has no duration to set the shadow against, which is the second option's error, because an image is not a substitute for the structure that makes the image mean anything. The fourth option is a common draft, but fronting the shadow clause would put the later event first and remove the order in which the reader feels the arrival.
questions.hint: Ask which clause supplies the measure the shadow is measured against.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what anaphora does to a series of clauses
questions.stem: Three consecutive lines of an invented poem read: "I did not knock. / I did not call his name down the stair. / I did not count them, the steps, all the way down." What is the repeated opening doing?

options.text: Stacking three refusals, so each line makes the refusal before it weigh more
Slowing the reading, so the reader must take three breaths to get to the end
options.misconception: attributes the effect to breath rate instead of to accumulated refusal

options.text: Showing the speaker is uncertain, since a repeated start implies hesitation
options.misconception: reads syntactic repetition as evidence of a wavering speaker

options.text: Marking a list, since the repeated words declare what kind of line this is
options.misconception: treats repetition as a category label rather than as a build

questions.explanation: Anaphora repeats a unit at the start of successive clauses, and the repetition makes each new clause an addition to the ones before it rather than a replacement. "I did not" is the frame, and what fills it escalates: a knock, a name, then a count, so the reader arrives at the last line with a weight the first line did not have. The tempting reading watches the breath instead of the content, and the fourth option treats the repetition as a label, but the words inside the frame are precisely what the frame is being asked to carry.
questions.hint: Ask what each new "I did not" adds to the one before it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: locate the effect of a break in a repeated pattern
questions.stem: Four lines: "We counted the crates in the yard. / We counted the salt rings on the table. / We counted the nails. / The rain began before we reached the door." What does the fourth line do after three lines that open the same way?

options.text: It breaks the pattern, so the counting stops and the interruption lands
It completes the pattern, since its subject is as countable as the others
options.misconception: hears a change of subject as one more item in the sequence

options.text: It explains the rain, since counting cannot keep a storm from starting
options.misconception: reads the last line as a cause offered for the weather

options.text: It criticises the counting, since rain spoils whatever it measures
options.misconception: takes a change of topic as an unspoken criticism of the speakers

questions.explanation: A reader who has met three identical openings knows exactly what the fourth line will open with, which means the fourth line's opening is itself an event. This one does not supply it, so the pattern is broken at the last moment, and the break is where the poem's real subject arrives. The tempting reading wants the break to keep counting, but rain is not a countable item, and the two readings that supply a motive, whether the counting caused the weather or the writer condemns it, are additions the text does not make.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader expects the fourth line to begin with.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish anaphora from a repeated whole line
questions.stem: A poem opens every stanza with the identical line "the sea was loud that year" and varies what follows it. What makes this a refrain rather than anaphora?

options.text: The whole line recurs intact, not a word or phrase at the front of clauses
The line comes first in each stanza, so it occupies an opening position
options.misconception: confuses a repeated position with a repeated fragment

options.text: The line is unchanged, where anaphora would vary whatever follows it
options.misconception: defines the difference as variation rather than as the extent of the repeat

options.text: The line carries the poem's subject, so it is a refrain by definition
options.misconception: assigns a label by thematic importance rather than by form

questions.explanation: Anaphora is a repetition of a unit at the openings of successive clauses or lines, and the repeated unit is usually short; a refrain repeats a whole line, often the same line, at the same structural point each time. So the difference is one of extent and placement rather than of mere recurrence, which is what the second and third options argue. The fourth option is a separate error, since a repeated line is a refrain whatever it is about, and a line's importance to the poem does not decide its form.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the line comes back, and where.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: identify an end-stopped line and state what its stop does
questions.stem: A passage reads "the ferryman's shoulder." and then, as a new line, "He had not looked up." Which line is end-stopped, and what does the stop do?

options.text: The first, and it seals the clause so the picture closes before it reopens
The second, and it closes the passage so the reader must stop with him
options.misconception: assigns the stop to the line that ends the passage

options.text: The first, and it prevents the reader from joining the two sentences at all
options.misconception: believes a line-ending stop blocks the connection to the next line

options.text: The second, and it shows the sentence was written to be read out loud
options.misconception: infers a purpose in performance from the position of a full stop

questions.explanation: An end-stopped line is one whose grammatical unit closes at the line's end, usually with terminal punctuation, so a reader can complete the thought before moving on. Here the first line completes a noun phrase and a period, so it closes; the second opens a new sentence, which is the opposite arrangement. The tempting reading confuses ending a line with ending a passage, and the fourth option invents a performance purpose that the typography does not carry, since nothing about a full stop tells a reader the sentence was meant to be spoken.
questions.hint: Ask which line's grammar finishes inside itself.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: locate the break that carries a verb across a line boundary
questions.stem: A poem runs: "The letters went out on the second of the month, / addressed to a firm that had moved in March, / and returned to me / stamped." Which break carries the verb across the line?

options.text: The one after "returned to me," where the verb still waits for its object
The one after "March," where the sentence keeps moving into the next line
options.misconception: names a break after an adjunct as the break that carries the verb

options.text: The one after "the month," which begins the sentence's second clause
options.misconception: treats the end of a subordinate time clause as the decisive break

options.text: The one after "stamped," which ends the poem on a participle
options.misconception: calls a final word a break that carries a verb onward

questions.explanation: Enjambment is a break made before a grammatical unit is finished, and the tell is that some part of the sentence is still owed. After "returned to me" the verb "returned" has an object it has not yet received, and "stamped" supplies it, so that break is the one doing the work. The other three breaks fall at points where the syntax is already complete enough to pause: after a time clause, after a prepositional phrase, and after a final participle that is not owed anything.
questions.hint: Ask after which line a word is still missing from the sentence.

questions.learningObjective: state what a break inside a compound sentence withholds
questions.stem: Two settings of one couplet are given. Version 1: "She shut the ledger. / The rain had not stopped." Version 2: "She shut the ledger, and the / rain had not stopped." What does Version 2's break withhold?

options.text: Whether the closing of the ledger and the rain belong to one action
Whether the rain was still falling when she rose from the table
options.misconception: believes the break conceals a fact about the rain's later state

options.text: Why she shut the ledger, which the second clause is meant to explain
options.misconception: expects the second line to supply a motive the first withholds

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a conceit more than a single metaphor
questions.stem: A poem describes a house for forty lines as a ship: a keel, a mast, a hold, a harbour, a chart. What makes this a conceit rather than one metaphor?

options.text: The comparison is sustained and developed, not dropped after a single line
House and ship are both things people own, so the comparison is exact
options.misconception: grounds a conceit in shared category instead of sustained development

options.text: The comparison is unexpected, since a house is not usually a vessel
options.misconception: takes unusualness of comparison as the entire definition of a conceit

options.text: The poem uses several figures, so the ship cannot be a simple metaphor
options.misconception: believes a conceit requires many figures rather than one developed one

questions.explanation: A conceit is a comparison that is kept up across a stretch of writing, so that each new detail has to be fitted to the terms already established and the comparison gets more specific as it goes. A metaphor, by contrast, can be established and abandoned in a line. That is why the second and fourth options fail: a shared category or a pile of figures is not what makes a conceit work, and the third option confuses being surprising, which a conceit may be, with being developed, which it must be.
questions.hint: Ask whether the comparison survives the second stanza.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: identify the line in which a conceit is developed rather than stated
questions.stem: Four lines: "The house kept one green lamp burning. / Its floors pitched when the north wind got under them. / In the cellar the winter casks complained. / Nobody had sailed her out of the strait." Which line shows the conceit being developed?

options.text: The third, since a complaining cask turns the cellar into a hold with a crew
The first, since it names the part the whole comparison is built on
options.misconception: treats a conceit's opening image as its developed use

options.text: The second, since the pitching floor carries the figure out into weather
options.misconception: credits an image of motion with developing the figure's second term

options.text: The fourth, since it says aloud that the house was never a ship
options.misconception: reads a closing denial as the poem's developed comparison

questions.explanation: Developing a conceit means finding a new detail that the established terms force the reader to reinterpret, not merely a detail that fits beside them. The first line states the lamp and the second adds motion, but the third is where the comparison has to work: casks that complain belong to a hold with a crew, so the cellar is re-read as a ship's lower space and the figure acquires a second application. The fourth line announces rather than develops, and the second option mistakes a conceit's foundation for its use.
questions.hint: Ask which line would be impossible if the ship were not the comparison.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: reconstruct the order in which a chain of dependent clauses must arrive
questions.stem: A printer has lost the order of one sentence's clauses. Restore them so the sentence opens with a time clause, the relative clause attaches to the last noun of the clause before it, and the main clause still comes last. The pieces: "he put out the lamp" / "where the dog, woken by the cart, would not leave" / "after the last visitor had gone" / "in the room at the back"

options.text: after the last visitor had gone
in the room at the back
where the dog, woken by the cart, would not leave
he put out the lamp

questions.explanation: A chain of dependent clauses has one order that satisfies all three conditions. The time clause has to open the sentence, the locative clause has to come next because the relative clause attaches to its final noun, and the main clause has to close, so the only arrangement that satisfies all three is opener, then locative, then relative, then main verb. The conditions are what fix the order rather than any sense of emphasis a reader might feel in the fragments, which is why the arrangement can be recovered even though no fragment indicates its own position.
questions.hint: Ask which piece can open the sentence, and which piece can close it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what a marker of likeness adds to a comparison
questions.stem: Two versions of a line: "The harbour was a bowl of cold pewter." and "The harbour lay like a bowl of cold pewter." What does the second version add to the first?

options.text: A marker of likeness, so the image is a resemblance, not an identity
A second comparison, so the reader now has both an identity and a likeness
options.misconception: counts the added preposition as an extra figure in one image

options.text: A caution, since like warns the reader the comparison may not hold
options.misconception: treats the marker of likeness as a hedge on the comparison's truth

options.text: Nothing, since the two versions carry the same image in the same order
options.misconception: denies that the grammatical form of a comparison can carry meaning

questions.explanation: A simile marks likeness with a word such as like or as, and a metaphor asserts identity by dropping the marker and using the copula or a related verb. The image is the same in both versions here, so what changes is the kind of claim being made: a resemblance the reader is invited to test against the harbour, rather than an identity the line simply states. The third option is the standard confusion, treating the marker as caution, and the fourth is wrong because grammatical form is not decoration; it is the difference between comparing and equating.
questions.hint: Ask which version leaves the reader room to doubt the comparison.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: identify the grammatical evidence that makes a comparison a metaphor
questions.stem: A poem has "the noon was a held breath" in one line and "her voice went through me like a wire" in the next. What makes the first of these a metaphor?

options.text: It equates noon with a breath, with no word joining them by likeness
It names a duration, and a duration is too abstract to be compared
options.misconception: believes an abstract subject cannot take a figurative comparison

options.text: It is short, and short lines are more often metaphors than similes
options.misconception: infers figure from line length rather than from the linking grammar

options.text: It comes before any marker of likeness appears in the poem
options.misconception: lets a poem's ordering of figures decide how one figure is classified

Here "was" asserts that the noon was a held breath, and no likeness-marker appears, so the identity is offered directly. The second and third options argue from the subject matter and the line's length, neither of which bears on the grammar, and the fourth confuses a poem's arrangement of figures with the class of any one of them.
questions.hint: Ask which word in each line does the joining.

questions.learningObjective: convert a metaphor into a simile without altering the image
questions.stem: A sentence reads "The land after the fire was a lung with nothing left to draw on." A writer wants the same image carried by a simile. Which revision does that?

questions.learningObjective: identify which two senses an image brings together
questions.stem: A line of an invented poem reads "the trumpet's edge went cold across the room." Which description of the line is accurate?

It reports two objects in the room, a trumpet and a cold, that both exist

options.text: It states that the room's temperature fell when the trumpet was played
options.misconception: takes a sensory crossing as a literal report about the room

questions.learningObjective: judge which sensory detail does the most work in a passage
questions.stem: Three lines: "The vinegar went through the room like a shout. / My aunt's hands smelled of it for a week. / I could not eat anything that tasted of a Thursday." Which detail does the most to fix the memory in place?

options.text: The third, since it fixes a taste to a weekday and so dates the refusal
The second, since a smell lasting a week is a longer fact than any image
options.misconception: ranks details by how long they last rather than by what they fix

options.misconception: values a line for its verbs and ignores the third line's precision

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: explain what giving an atmosphere a feeling does
questions.stem: A novelist writes, "The house had a smell like a kept grudge." What does giving an atmosphere a grudge do that calling it stale could not?

options.text: It gives the smell a history of withheld feeling, which staleness does not
It tells the reader the house had actually been quarrelled with
options.misconception: reads a comparison to a feeling as a report of a real dispute

options.text: It warns the reader that something is wrong with the family who lived there
options.misconception: jumps from an image to an inference the line makes about people

options.text: It makes the smell more pleasant, since a grudge is a mild household emotion
options.misconception: assumes figurative language always improves on the plain word

questions.explanation: A grudge is something held and not said, so borrowing the word for a smell gives the smell a history of feeling that has been kept rather than expressed. "Stale" could only say how long the smell had been there, so the comparison is doing a different job from a plain descriptor: it characterises the atmosphere as the residue of something unsaid. questions.stem: A narrator writes, "You will have noticed that the door was open, and that nobody has said so." What does the address do to the reader's position in the story?

It removes the reader, since a second person is not a character who can be blamed
options.misconception: believes a change of person removes the reader from the action

options.text: It proves the narrator unreliable, since a narrator cannot know what you noticed
options.misconception: treats an address as a claim about the reader's mind that fails

options.text: It dates the book, since second-person narration is a modern invention
options.misconception: dates a narrating choice as though it were a period marker

Certainty, since an untagged thought cannot be mistaken for anyone else's

options.misconception: treats a narrative mode as a way of sparing a character

The delayed main clause, since the reader is held from the outcome the longest

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: explain how a recurring image and a withheld ending work together
questions.stem: A story repeats the image of an unlatched gate in five of its eleven chapters, always in the same two words, never explained. Its last chapter leaves the gate open and closes without saying whether anyone passes through it. Explain how the image and the ending work together, and what a reader who notices both has that a reader who notices neither does not.

answer.exemplar: The two work together because the image accumulates a meaning the ending then declines to confirm. Each appearance of "the unlatched gate" adds a little pressure without settling anything, so by the last chapter the phrase carries everything the story has withheld about leaving, coming back, and being undecided, and it carries it in two flat words the reader has read five times. The ending then refuses to say whether anyone passes through, which would settle the question the image has been holding open, so the image is left doing the work an ending would normally do. A reader who notices both therefore experiences an ending as a withheld decision rather than as an absence, and can say exactly what was withheld and by what means. A reader who notices neither takes the repeated phrase for a detail of the house and reads the last chapter as a story that stopped, which is a coherent reading of the same words and not the one the text has built.

questions.explanation: A good explanation of this kind has to name the two mechanisms separately before it can say how they interact, because the interaction is the part that is not visible from either alone. The accumulating image is doing the work of withheld information: each recurrence adds pressure without resolving anything, and a reader's memory of the earlier appearances is what gives the last one its charge. The withheld ending is doing the work of withheld decision: it removes the event that would have settled the question, and in removing it hands the closing function back to the image. Putting those together, the text's final effect is neither a resolution nor a simple stop, and a reader who has both pieces in hand can describe that effect in terms of the specific device that produced it, which is what the answer above does. The temptation in an explanation item is to praise the story or to generalise about endings, and neither helps a reader, because neither says what to look for on the next page.
questions.hint: Ask what the phrase has been made to hold, and what the ending refuses to give it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: say what evidence would settle a claim about a passage
questions.stem: A student claims that a poem's final line is hopeful. The poem's last three lines are: "and the light came back off the water, / and the boats went out, / and I did not follow." Explain what from the poem would settle whether the claim holds, and why the student's evidence so far is not enough.

answer.exemplar: The claim would be settled by what the line's word is doing, which is why the student's reading of it is the whole question. Hope in this poem has to attach to somebody, and the last line says only that the speaker stayed ashore, so the settling evidence is the poem's account of what staying cost him and what the going boats were for. If the earlier lines make the boats a duty or an escape, the last line is a refusal, and the claim fails; if they make the boats a loss he had accepted, the last line is a choice he can live with, and the claim holds. The student's evidence so far is the word "back" in the second-to-last line, which is a fact about light on water and says nothing about the speaker, so it cannot support a claim about his state without the intervening account of who the boats matter to.

questions.explanation: An explanation about evidence has to do two things: say what kind of evidence would settle the claim, and say why the evidence in hand cannot settle it. The first is a question of what the claim is about, and this claim is about a person's state of mind, so the relevant evidence cannot be a description of light on a river. It has to be whatever the poem says about what the boats are and whom they matter to, because that is the only place a hope or a despair can be located. The second is a question of scale, and the mistake being made is a mismatch of scales: a word is being used to settle a claim about a person, when a word can only settle a claim about a description. Explaining that mismatch is more useful than ruling on the claim, because it tells a writer what to go and find.
questions.hint: Ask who the hope would have to be for, and where the poem says.
